newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: Kin of jailed UK nurses visit them again in Saudi.
newsitem.headline: Kin of jailed UK nurses visit them again in Saudi.

text.p: Two British nurses charged with murdering an Australian colleague in Saudi Arabia appeared in good health but were finding life at the women's section of a Dammam prison difficult, a relative said on Monday.
The two Britons, Lucille McLauchlan, 31, and Deborah Parry, 41, were imprisoned in the eastern Saudi city of Dammam on December 20 and charged with murdering Yvonne Gilford, 55.

Under Islamic sharia law, the two could face public beheading if found guilty of premeditated murder by a panel of three judges. Defendants have the right of appeal to two other five-judge panels before a final verdict is passed.

The two women saw their relatives on Sunday for the first time in what Jonathan Ashby, Parry's brother-in-law, said was an emotional reunion in two separate rooms for "the good part of two hours". He was accompanied by Parry's uncle Terry Knight.
They saw them again on Monday.
"We would like to say that we visited them again today (Monday) and they both are well...They are very well treated," Jonathan Ashby, Parry's brother-in-law, told reporters.
The relatives also met British consul in the Saudi capital Riyadh, Tim Lamb, for what he said was a "private discussion."
Ashby declined further comment but insisted both women were innocent. Other relatives refused to talk to reporters.
Ashby said earlier that Parry was wearing a long black robe, or abaya, which women in the conservative kingdom must wear, but her head was not covered, as custom dictates. She was not handcuffed.

"She appeared to be well," he told Reuters earlier by telephone from Dammam. "She is finding it difficult, which is obvious. She did not ask for anything...but said they (the two women) were finding it difficult...," he added.
He said a Saudi policeman was "present for some of the time" and that the two women appeared to be held in the same cell.

McLauchlan's parents have remained tight-lipped since their arrival in Damman on Saturday. But her father, Stan, was quoted in the Saudi paper Arab News on Monday as saying conditions in the jail were "okay" and that the visit was to "see Lucy, reassure, comfort and stand by her".
Ashby said the group did not know how long they would stay in the kingdom. "We are taking it day by day."

A British Foreign Office spokesman said on Sunday a lawyer representing the two, Michael Dark, and a British consul, Lawson Ross, were also at the prison on Sunday. Ross delivered personal articles for the nurses.

Ashby said the relatives and the two nurses were still struggling to understand the Islamic sharia law applied in the kingdom. "We don't fully understand the legal system here...The lawyers are explaining things to us."

In the event of guilty verdicts, Gilford's family could spare the lives of the two and ask for financial recompense known as blood money instead of the death sentence. Gilford's family in Australia have ruled out a clemency appeal.
Legal experts said that if found guilty of manslaughter the two women would not be condemned to death.
Gilford was stabbed four times, battered with a hammer and smothered in her dormitory at the King Fahd military medical complex in the eastern oil city of Dhahran on December 11.
Saudi police have said the two confessed to the murders and the confessions were filed with three judges.

But the law firm Salah al-Hejailan said last week after a visit to the two Britons that they withdrew their confessions and one of them retracted a statement that she had a lesbian relationship with the victim.
